```{r}
source("_common.R")
source("_figures.R")
# a CHD cohort simulated by the module: the people of the figures below
sc_chd <- load_scenario(lib, "chd_incidence")
coh <- simulate_study(sc_chd, "chd", "cohort", 4000, sc_chd$order, seed = 7, key = FALSE)$data_raw
pick <- function(d, n_ev, n_no, seed = 1) {
    set.seed(seed)
    rbind(d[sample(which(d$chd == 1), n_ev), ], d[sample(which(d$chd == 0), n_no), ])
}
```

In an observational study the investigator does not decide who is exposed.
Exposed and unexposed people may differ in other ways that affect the outcome
(**confounding**), people may enter the study in ways related to exposure and
outcome (**selection bias**), and exposure or outcome may be measured with error
(**information bias**). Each design is a way of sampling a population. The
analysis has to match that sampling, and the [causal diagram](guide-dags.qmd)
says what to adjust for.

| design | samples | measures | main model |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cross-sectional | a population at one time | prevalence, prevalence ratio or OR | logistic or linear regression |
| Ecological | groups (regions) | rates and means of groups | regression on group summaries |
| Cohort | people free of the outcome, followed | risk, rate, hazard | Cox, Poisson, logistic |
| Case-control | cases, and a sample of non-cases | odds ratio | logistic regression |
| Matched case-control | cases, and controls matched to each | odds ratio within sets | conditional logistic regression |
| Nested case-control | a cohort's cases, controls from their risk sets | hazard ratio | conditional logistic regression |
| Case-cohort | a cohort's cases, a random subcohort | hazard ratio | weighted Cox regression |
| Prognosis | patients from diagnosis | survival, cumulative incidence, HR | Kaplan-Meier, Cox, competing risks |

## Cross-sectional study

**What it is.** Exposure and outcome measured at the same time in a sample of a
population: a health survey, a screening programme.

**Estimates.** Prevalence, and prevalence ratios or odds ratios between groups.

::: {#fig-cross-sectional}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
xs_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    set.seed(3)
    d <- data.frame(start = runif(40, 0, 10))
    d$long <- seq_len(40) %% 2 == 0
    d$end <- d$start + ifelse(d$long, rexp(40, 1 / 3.5), rexp(40, 1 / 0.6))
    d <- d[order(d$start), ]; d$row <- seq_len(nrow(d))
    d$prevalent <- d$start <= 6 & d$end >= 6
    d$kind <- ifelse(d$long, "long episodes", "short episodes")
    ggplot(d) + annotate("rect", xmin = 5.9, xmax = 6.1, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = p$role[["exposure"]], alpha = 0.25) +
        geom_segment(aes(x = start, xend = pmin(end, 12), y = row, yend = row, linetype = kind, alpha = prevalent),
                     colour = p$role[["outcome"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
        annotate("text", x = 6.2, y = 41.5, label = "survey", hjust = 0, colour = p$fg, size = 3.6) +
        scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 0.3, `TRUE` = 1), guide = "none") +
        scale_linetype_manual(values = c("long episodes" = "solid", "short episodes" = "11"), name = NULL) +
        scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 12)) + labs(x = "calendar time", y = NULL) + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(xs_fig)
```
Episodes of a disease in a population (one line each). A survey sees only the episodes in progress on its day (bright): the long ones are overrepresented, so a prevalent sample mixes the causes of getting the disease with the causes of keeping it.
:::

**Strengths.** Quick and cheap; describes the burden of a condition and plans
services; studies many exposures and outcomes at once.

**Limitations.** Exposure and outcome are measured together, so their time
order is often unknown (does low activity cause depression, or the reverse?).
Prevalent cases over-represent long-lasting disease (@fig-cross-sectional).
Survivors only: people who died of the disease are missing.

**Analysis.** Prevalence with its confidence interval; logistic regression
(odds ratios) or, better for common outcomes, a log-binomial or Poisson model
with robust errors (prevalence ratios); linear regression for continuous
outcomes.

**Interpretation.** An odds ratio of 1.8 for diabetes with obesity means the
odds of *having* diabetes are 1.8 times higher in obese people with the same
values of the other variables in the model. It is not a risk of *developing*
diabetes, and with a common outcome it overstates the prevalence ratio.

**In studysim.** *Blood pressure in US adults* or *Diabetes in Pima women*,
cross-sectional design.

## Ecological study

**What it is.** The units are groups (regions, countries, years), with only group
summaries: the rate of the outcome, the mean or percentage of the exposure.

**Estimates.** The association between group summaries. It is not the effect on
individuals.

::: {#fig-ecological}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
eco_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    set.seed(11)
    reg <- data.frame(region = LETTERS[1:6], mx = seq(2, 7, length.out = 6))
    ind <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(6), function(g) {
        x <- rnorm(25, reg$mx[g], 0.7)
        data.frame(region = reg$region[g], x = x, y = 2 + 1.6 * reg$mx[g] - 0.9 * (x - reg$mx[g]) + rnorm(25, 0, 0.5))
    }))
    mean_y <- tapply(ind$y, ind$region, mean)
    reg$my <- mean_y[reg$region]
    ggplot(ind, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(aes(colour = region), alpha = 0.35, size = 1.4) +
        geom_smooth(aes(group = region, colour = region), method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x, linewidth = 0.8) +
        geom_smooth(data = reg, aes(mx, my), method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x, colour = p$fg, linetype = "dashed") +
        geom_point(data = reg, aes(mx, my), colour = p$fg, size = 3.2, shape = 21, fill = p$panel, stroke = 1.2) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = grDevices::hcl.colors(6, "Dark 3"), guide = "none") +
        labs(x = "exposure", y = "outcome") + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(eco_fig)
```
The ecological fallacy. Across regions (open circles, dashed line) more exposure goes with more of the outcome; within every region (coloured lines) the individual association is the opposite. Something that differs between regions confounds the regional comparison.
:::

**Strengths.** Uses routine data (registries, censuses), so it is fast and cheap;
studies exposures that only exist at group level (policies, water hardness, air
pollution); good for generating hypotheses [@morgenstern1995].

**Limitations.** The **ecological fallacy** (@fig-ecological): a group-level
association need not hold for individuals, because regions differ in many
things at once (contextual confounding) and nobody knows who in a region was
exposed and who fell ill. Group summaries also hide non-linear effects.

**Analysis.** Regression of the regional rate on regional means and percentages,
weighted by population size (Poisson with the population as offset for counts).

**Interpretation.** A coefficient per percentage point of smokers is the change
in the regional rate between regions that differ by one point. It is not the
risk ratio of smoking.

**In studysim.** *Water hardness and mortality* or *Dietary fat and breast
cancer*, ecological design: compare the regional slope with the individual
effect in the answer key.

## Cohort study

**What it is.** People free of the outcome are classified by exposure and
followed until the outcome, a competing event, loss to follow-up or the end of
the study.

::: {#fig-cohort}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
d <- rbind(transform(pick(coh[coh$smoking == "current", ], 4, 9, 1), group = "smokers"),
           transform(pick(coh[coh$smoking == "never", ], 2, 11, 2), group = "never smoked"))
d <- data.frame(start = 0, end = d$time, event = d$chd, group = d$group)
both(timeline_fig, d, xlab = "years since entry")
```
Twenty-six people of a simulated cohort (*Coronary heart disease incidence*), each followed from entry: a cross is a coronary event, a bar the end of follow-up without one (loss or end of the study).
:::

**Estimates.** Risks (cumulative incidence), rates and hazards in each exposure
group, and their ratios and differences.

**Strengths.** Exposure is measured before the outcome, so the time order is
clear and recall cannot be biased by the outcome; several outcomes of one
exposure can be studied; it gives absolute risks.

**Limitations.** Large and long for rare or slow outcomes (the coronary cohort
of 3,000 people has about 250 events in 10 years); losses to follow-up that
depend on prognosis bias the results (**informative censoring**); confounding,
as in any observational design; exposure can change during follow-up.

**Analysis.** Kaplan-Meier curves and the log-rank test; Cox regression for
hazard ratios adjusted for confounders; Poisson regression of counts with log
person-time as offset for rates; logistic regression only when everybody is
followed for the same period.

**Interpretation.** A hazard ratio of 1.6 for smoking means that at any time
during follow-up, among those still free of the event, smokers have 1.6 times
the event rate of non-smokers with the same values of the adjustment variables.
It assumes the ratio is constant over time (check proportional hazards).

**Two traps.** A treatment that starts during follow-up must not be analysed as
if it were present from entry: the treated had to survive until they started it
(**immortal time**), and the treatment looks protective even when useless
[@suissa2008]. Treat it as a time-dependent variable, or compare from a
landmark time. And adjusting for something that happens *after* the exposure
(a mediator, or a consequence of the outcome) changes the question; see
[Causal diagrams](guide-dags.qmd).

**In studysim.** *Coronary heart disease incidence*, cohort; *Biases* ▸
*Informative loss to follow-up* and *Treatment started during follow-up*.

### Prognosis and competing risks

A **prognosis** study is a cohort of patients from diagnosis or treatment,
recruited over several years (staggered entry), to describe survival and its
predictors. When patients can die of something else before the outcome of
interest, that death is a **competing event**. A Cox model that censors it
estimates the **cause-specific hazard ratio**, a valid measure of the effect on
the rate of the event. But 1 − Kaplan-Meier, which treats the deaths from other
causes as if those patients could still have the event, overstates its
**cumulative incidence** (@fig-competing).

::: {#fig-competing}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
sc_bc <- load_scenario(lib, "breast_cancer_prognosis")
pr <- simulate_study(sc_bc, "bc_death", "prognosis", 6000, sc_bc$order, seed = 3, key = FALSE)$data_raw
cif <- function(d, grp) {
    km <- survival::survfit(survival::Surv(time, bc_death == 1) ~ 1, data = d)
    aj <- survival::survfit(survival::Surv(time, factor(bc_death, levels = 0:2)) ~ 1, data = d)
    oth <- summary(aj, times = 10)$pstate[, 3]
    lab <- sprintf("%s: other deaths %.0f%% by 10 years", grp, 100 * oth)
    data.frame(time = c(km$time, aj$time), value = c(1 - km$surv, aj$pstate[, 2]), group = lab,
               curve = rep(c("1 - Kaplan-Meier (competing deaths censored)", "cumulative incidence (Aalen-Johansen)"),
                           c(length(km$time), length(aj$time))))
}
ci <- rbind(cif(pr, "all patients"), cif(pr[pr$age >= 75, ], "aged 75 and over"))
ci$group <- factor(ci$group, levels = unique(ci$group))
cr_fig <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    ggplot(ci, aes(time, value, colour = curve)) + geom_step(linewidth = 1) + facet_wrap(~group) +
        scale_colour_manual(values = unname(p$role[c("outcome", "exposure")]), name = NULL) +
        scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10)) +
        labs(x = "years from diagnosis", y = "death from breast cancer") +
        theme_plot(mode) + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
both(cr_fig)
```
Deaths from breast cancer in a simulated prognosis cohort with deaths from other causes (*Breast cancer prognosis*). 1 − Kaplan-Meier overstates the proportion who die of breast cancer, and the more so the more patients die of something else first.
:::

## Case-control study

**What it is.** All (or a random sample of) the cases of a disease arising in a
source population, and a sample of people from the same population who are not
cases (controls); exposure is then measured in both, usually looking back.

::: {#fig-case-control}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
set.seed(5)
pop <- data.frame(x = runif(600), y = runif(600))
pop$status <- ifelse(runif(600) < 0.04, "case", "non-case")
ctrl <- sample(which(pop$status == "non-case"), 2 * sum(pop$status == "case"))
pop2 <- rbind(transform(pop, panel = "source population", chosen = NA),
              transform(pop, panel = "the study: every case, 2 controls each", chosen = status == "case" | seq_len(600) %in% ctrl))
both(sample_fig, pop2)
```
A case-control study samples by outcome: all the cases (red) of the source population and a random sample of the non-cases. The proportion of cases in the study is set by the design, so it estimates odds ratios, not risks.
:::

**Estimates.** The exposure odds ratio, which equals the disease odds ratio.
With controls sampled from those still at risk when each case occurs (risk-set
sampling, as in a nested case-control study) it estimates the rate ratio, with
no rare-disease assumption. Otherwise it approximates the risk ratio when the
disease is rare.

**Strengths.** Efficient for rare diseases and long latencies (a few hundred
cases instead of a cohort of a hundred thousand); many exposures can be studied
for one disease; fast.

**Limitations.** Controls must come from the population that gave rise to the
cases: hospital controls admitted for diseases related to the exposure distort
the odds ratio (**selection bias**). Exposure recalled after the diagnosis can
be reported differently by cases (**recall bias**). No absolute risks unless the
sampling fractions are known.

**Analysis.** Logistic regression with case status as the outcome, adjusted for
confounders. The intercept is meaningless (it reflects the sampling), but the
odds ratios are valid.

**Interpretation.** An odds ratio of 7.7 for smoking 1-14 cigarettes a day means
the odds of lung cancer are 7.7 times higher than in never smokers with the same
age and sex. For a rare disease it reads as the rate ratio.

**In studysim.** *Lung cancer and smoking* or *Oesophageal cancer*,
case-control; *Biases* ▸ *Recall bias* and *Controls selected by exposure*,
ticking smoking as the exposure.

### Matched case-control

Each case gets controls with the same values of some confounders (age, sex,
hospital). Matching makes the groups comparable on those variables and can
increase efficiency, but it **must be kept in the analysis**: conditional
logistic regression compares each case with its own controls. An ordinary
logistic regression of matched data is biased towards the null, the effect of a
matching variable cannot be estimated, and matching on something caused by the
exposure (overmatching) removes part of the effect.

### Nested case-control and case-cohort

Both sample a cohort whose follow-up is already recorded, to avoid measuring an
expensive exposure (a biomarker in stored blood) on everybody.

::: {#fig-nested}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
d <- pick(coh, 4, 16, 3)
d <- d[order(-d$time), ]
d <- data.frame(start = 0, end = d$time, event = d$chd, group = "cohort member")
case_row <- which(d$event == 1)[2]
t_case <- d$end[case_row]
at_risk <- which(d$end >= t_case)
set.seed(2); controls <- sample(setdiff(at_risk, case_row), 2)
both(timeline_fig, d, xlab = "years since entry", highlight = c(case_row, controls),
     marks = function(p) list(geom_vline(xintercept = t_case, linetype = "dashed", colour = p$role[["outcome"]]),
                              annotate("point", x = t_case, y = controls, shape = 21, size = 4, colour = p$role[["control"]], stroke = 1.3),
                              annotate("text", x = t_case + 0.15, y = nrow(d) + 0.8, label = "case's event time: its risk set", hjust = 0, colour = p$fg, size = 3.5)))
```
Nested case-control: for each case (here the highlighted one), controls are drawn from its **risk set**, the people still followed and free of the event at the case's event time (lines crossing the dashed line). A control can later become a case.
:::

- **Nested case-control**: for each case, a few controls from its risk set
  (@fig-nested). Analysed with conditional logistic regression on the risk
  sets, it estimates the hazard ratio of the full cohort.
- **Case-cohort** [@prentice1986]: a random **subcohort** chosen at the start,
  plus every case. The same subcohort serves several outcomes. The analysis is a
  Cox model weighted for the sampling (Prentice or Lin-Ying weights) with a
  robust variance; it estimates the hazard ratio.

**In studysim.** *Relapse of Wilms tumour*: nested case-control and case-cohort
from the same cohort.

## What to remember

| design | biggest threat | protect with |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-sectional | unknown time order; prevalent cases | incident cases, clear definitions of when exposure happened |
| Ecological | ecological fallacy | individual data; use only for hypotheses |
| Cohort | confounding; informative loss to follow-up; immortal time | adjustment chosen with a DAG; complete follow-up; time-dependent exposures |
| Case-control | selection of controls; recall bias | population controls from the source population; records instead of recall |
| Matched | analysis that ignores matching; overmatching | conditional logistic regression; match only on confounders |
